A Grammy winner had security throw a grieving mom out of his concert for falling asleep. The box office numbers for that night just came out, and two-thirds of the seats were empty.

He kicked out one of the people who actually showed up.

That's Burna Boy at Red Rocks, outside Denver, a year ago. Two summers before that, he packed 41,800 people into Citi Field and became the first African artist ever to sell out a stadium in the US. This is a guy who's supposed to fill arenas without trying.

The woman later explained she'd just lost her daughter's father and went to the show to cheer herself up. She was sitting up front, she dozed off, and he stopped the concert until she was gone. When people got mad, he compared himself to a pilot kicking a rowdy passenger off a plane.

Ten days later came Houston. Toyota Center, the same building he'd headlined in 2022, sold 44%. He was in Dallas two nights after that, on stage apologizing and calling the whole thing a slip of the tongue. By Thanksgiving, Minneapolis had been pulled from Ticketmaster less than 24 hours before showtime, and his Chicago date went with it.

Now look at when those empty seats actually happened. Red Rocks sold 35% of its tickets, and it was opening night, on sale since June. That number was locked in before anybody had heard of a sleeping fan. Oakland played six days later and filled 37% while charging the highest average ticket on the North American run, about $122. People were already passing on this tour before he ever stopped the music, and the sleeping fan just gave everybody a story to explain the empty seats.

Add up the North American dates and the tour grossed about $6 million, roughly half of what his 2024 run through the same continent pulled in.

When the backlash hit, he went online and said he'd gladly be cancelled, after a show where two out of every three seats had already done it for him.
